blocks.text: Module 1 constructs the malware-loader log collection used by TemporalKG from the publicly available WinMET dataset. The workflow uses the original sandbox reports as its data source and applies the project's LoaderFilter tool to select loader-related candidates from the broader malware corpus. The selected reports are then supplied to Module 2 for subsequent processing. LoaderFilter performs local filtering and preparation of existing reports; the sandbox traces originate from WinMET. [S1, S2]
a) Primary data source and collection scope

WinMET, short for Windows Malware Execution Traces, is published on Zenodo by Raducu et al. The referenced release is version v3, published on 25 July 2025, with DOI 10.5281/zenodo.16414116. It contains 31,844 CAPE-generated execution traces distributed across five archives. The JSON reports record process activity, WinAPI and system-call sequences, arguments, return values, and accessed operating-system resources. [S1]

The collection scope of this study covers all five WinMET volumes. Their extracted JSON reports provide the local inputs to the filtering workflow. The published total describes the source dataset; the downstream collection consists of the reports retained by the project-specific candidate selection. The filtering task selects loader-related reports within a malware corpus, rather than establishing a malware-versus-benign classification.
b) Label metadata and report matching

WinMET supplies three label files alongside the trace archives. The consensus file referenced in the source link contains label metadata rather than the execution logs themselves. Their roles are summarized below. [S1]

rows: Both label assignments for each trace.

blocks.text: LoaderFilter associates these metadata records with local reports using sample hashes obtained from valid report filenames and/or target metadata. It preserves separate identifiers for a source location, report content, and malware sample. The report identifier is calculated from the report's SHA-256 digest, whereas the sample hash identifies the analyzed binary. When the filename and target hashes disagree, the tool records an identity conflict rather than silently treating them as the same sample. [S2]

The label-loading logic retains CAPE and AVClass observations separately and reconciles them with the consensus index. A consensus entry can supplement a missing mapping. If it disagrees with an existing mapping, the discrepancy and its provenance remain recorded. Consequently, use of the consensus file does not mean that both labeling sources necessarily agree on every report. [S3]
c) Filtering the malware corpus for loader candidates

The local tool discovers JSON reports from the configured input directories and builds an inventory linked to the label metadata. Its bundled seed taxonomy contains eight canonical families: smokeloader, guloader, sload, gcleaner, upatre, modiloader, privateloader, and customerloader. Labels are normalized by removing surrounding whitespace and applying case folding, followed by explicit aliases defined in the taxonomy. This provides a consistent comparison between the metadata labels and the configured family names. [S2, S3]

At the inventory stage, a report is a seed candidate when at least one relevant label maps to a seed family. The broader candidate set also retains configured generic or review labels and conflicts between the mapping files and consensus index. These cases are recorded through reasons such as seed_label, generic_label_review, and label_index_conflict. Label agreement, disagreement, and missing values are retained as separate inventory information. The selection therefore preserves uncertain reports for further analysis rather than equating every candidate with a confirmed loader execution. [S3]

The tool also supports evidence-mode screening of CAPE reports. In this mode, the parser incrementally reads process records, selected API-call evidence, detections, and extracted or dropped artifact metadata. Additional candidate reasons can arise from loader-family detections within a report or delivery-related behavior. Scanning scope remains distinct from export selection: candidates limits evidence scanning to the initial candidate set, while all permits screening across the discovered collection. These are implementation capabilities; the export rule used for the study is specified below. [S2, S4]
d) Selection rule and downstream report collection

The collection passed to Module 2 uses the candidates export selection. The corresponding implementation retains sources marked is_candidate, including seed-family matches and the additional review reasons described above. It does not require the stricter loader_run_observed decision used by the separate observed selection. Thus, the resulting collection is a loader-related candidate subset of WinMET. This inclusion criterion preserves the distinction between family-label evidence, a reason for further inspection, and supported evidence of runtime loader execution. [S3, S5]

For report-level export, LoaderFilter copies the selected original JSON reports and verifies their SHA-256 values. The export manifest records report and sample identifiers, source information, and the effective decision, while accompanying metadata records the selection rule. Retaining the original reports preserves their telemetry for the next module. Internal facts.jsonl and processes.jsonl files support filtering and inspection, but the selected fact representation is not a replacement for the complete API-call stream in the source report. [S4, S5]

Report-level selection also does not imply that every process or API call in a retained report belongs exclusively to a loader. A selected sandbox report can retain other execution context. Likewise, exclusion from the seed taxonomy alone does not establish that a report is benign or definitively unrelated to loader activity. These distinctions define how the filtered collection should be interpreted in later analysis. [S3, S4]

The implementation preserves inventory manifests, processing statuses, configuration snapshots, and SQLite run state. Evidence-mode processing adds extracted evidence and quality flags. Parsing checks report structure and resource limits, records malformed or unsupported inputs, and detects changes to a source file during reading. The run-level quality checks examine identifiers, fingerprints, evidence integrity, manifest consistency, and decision prerequisites. These mechanisms support traceability between the original WinMET reports and the filtered collection; they do not by themselves establish the accuracy or completeness of loader identification. [S2, S4, S6]

The output of Module 1 is therefore the selected collection of existing WinMET reports, together with records explaining its selection and provenance. Subsequent telemetry normalization and transition construction belong to Module 2. [S5, S7]
